title: PyTorch Quiz
description: Revisit the key ideas in PyTorch. Read each choice carefully. You can try the quiz again after reviewing the lessons.

questions.question: What does this tensor contain?
questions.explanation: A PyTorch tensor stores numbers with a shape and a data type. torch.tensor makes one from a small Python list. The output is [2, 4, 6]. tolist returns ordinary Python values for easy inspection.

questions.question: How many total values are here?
questions.explanation: Shape gives the size of each dimension. ndim tells you how many dimensions there are. The output is (2, 2) 2. The tensor is a two-by-two table with two dimensions.

questions.question: Which dtype is requested?
questions.explanation: A dtype specifies how numbers are represented. Floating-point tensors are commonly used for model calculations and gradients. The output is torch.float32. Both values use that type.

questions.question: What is the first output value?
questions.explanation: Tensor arithmetic can combine matching positions. Shapes must match or follow broadcasting rules. The output is [4, 6]. The first values add together and so do the second values.

questions.question: What does @ mean here?
questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication combines rows with columns. The inner dimensions must match. It is different from element-wise multiplication. The result is 11.0 because 1 times 3 plus 2 times 4 equals 11. @ performs matrix multiplication.

questions.question: Which shape can hold six values?
questions.explanation: reshape changes the layout of a tensor while keeping the same number of values. The output is [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]. Six values fit two rows of three.

questions.question: What does x.grad hold?
questions.explanation: requires_grad asks PyTorch to track operations for automatic differentiation. backward fills the gradient of the scalar result with respect to the input. The result is 6.0. The local slope of x squared at 3 is twice 3.

questions.question: What does no_grad disable here?
questions.explanation: torch.no_grad runs operations without building a gradient-tracking graph. This is useful when you only need predictions. The result is False. The output is not tracked for a backward calculation.

questions.question: What does Linear(2, 1) expect per row?
questions.explanation: nn.Linear combines input features into output values using learned weights and a bias. Two inputs can produce one output. The output shape is (1, 1). Its numeric value depends on initial random weights.

questions.question: What does ReLU do to negative values?
questions.explanation: A sequential model applies layers in order. An activation such as ReLU keeps positive values and changes negative values to zero. The model produces shape (1, 1). The middle layer lets the model represent more than one plain linear transformation.

questions.question: Which line updates weights?
questions.explanation: A training step clears old gradients, computes loss, finds new gradients and updates weights. Each step has a separate job. The check prints True because squared-error loss is nonnegative. One update is only a demonstration, not a trained reliable model.

questions.question: Does eval disable gradient tracking by itself?
questions.explanation: model.eval switches training-sensitive layers to evaluation behaviour. Use it with no_grad when making ordinary evaluation predictions. The shape is (1, 1). This model is untrained; the example shows the evaluation procedure, not an accurate prediction.
